subject: Economics
topic: Foreign trade and BoP — mixed tiers
description: Balance of trade vs balance of payments, FTA, FTP, India's top exports/imports, currency

questions.stem: 'Balance of Trade' (BoT) is the difference between a country's:

options.option_text: Gross income and expenditure
Visible exports and visible imports of goods (NOT services)
Foreign reserves and foreign debt
Government revenue and expenditure

questions.explanation: BoT considers ONLY visible (merchandise/goods) trade. Balance of Payments (BoP) is broader: BoT + invisible trade (services, transfers, factor income) + capital account. India typically runs a TRADE DEFICIT (imports goods worth more than it exports — oil + gold + electronics drive imports). But a SURPLUS in services (IT, BPO, consultancy) helps narrow Current Account Deficit. CAD = BoT + Invisibles. India's CAD usually 1-3% of GDP.

questions.stem: India's BIGGEST single import item by value (typically) is:

options.option_text: Gold
Crude petroleum (and petroleum products)
Coal
Electronics

questions.explanation: Crude oil — India's largest single import (~25-30% of total imports by value, ~$130-150 B/year). India imports ~85% of its crude oil needs. Top suppliers in 2024-25: Russia (largest after Ukraine war discounts), Iraq, Saudi Arabia, UAE, USA. Other major imports: gold (~$40-50 B), electronics (smartphones, semiconductors), coal & coke, petroleum products, fertilisers. The trade deficit shrinks when crude prices fall or rupee strengthens.

questions.stem: India's TOP TWO export items by value are typically (FY 2024-25):

options.option_text: Diamonds and tea
Engineering goods + petroleum products (mineral fuels)
Spices and gems
Textiles and machinery

questions.explanation: India's top exports — Engineering goods (~25% — automotive, machinery, iron & steel), Petroleum products (refined products to Africa/SE Asia, ~13%), Electronics (smartphones now top — Apple Make-in-India contribution; ~6-7%), Pharmaceutical products (~6%), Gems & Jewellery (cut diamonds, ~6%), Chemicals, Textiles & Apparel, Agriculture (rice, marine products, spices, tea). Total goods exports ~$430-450 B (FY 2024-25). Services exports ~$340-350 B.

questions.stem: Foreign Trade Policy (FTP) of India is announced by which ministry?

options.option_text: Finance Ministry
Ministry of Commerce and Industry (DGFT)
External Affairs
RBI

questions.explanation: FTP — issued by Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) under Ministry of Commerce and Industry. Latest FTP — 1 April 2023 (replaced FTP 2015-20 which had multiple extensions). New FTP is 'dynamic and responsive' — no fixed end date. Key thrusts — districts as export hubs, e-commerce exports, MSME support, ₹2,000 crore RoDTEP scheme for tax remission, Towns of Export Excellence (TEEs).

questions.stem: Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) signed by India in recent years include those with — which is INCORRECT?

options.option_text: UAE (CEPA, 2022)
Australia (ECTA, 2022)
Brazil (BRICS-FTA, 2024)
EFTA — Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein (TEPA, 2024)

questions.explanation: India has NOT signed an FTA with Brazil. BRICS doesn't have an FTA framework — it's a political/economic grouping. India's recent FTAs: India-UAE CEPA (Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, May 2022), India-Australia ECTA (December 2022 — first goods deal with a developed country), India-EFTA TEPA (March 2024, signed; effective 2025), India-UK FTA (under negotiation). India withdrew from RCEP (2019). India-EU FTA still under negotiation since 2007.

questions.stem: India's largest single trading partner in 2024-25 is:

options.option_text: China
United States
Saudi Arabia
Russia

questions.explanation: USA — India's largest two-way trading partner since FY 2021-22 ($120+ B in 2024-25). Trade is in India's favour (surplus). China is India's largest IMPORT source (~$100 B) but exports are smaller — net trade is in China's favour. UAE is third (boosted by CEPA). Russia surged after 2022 due to discounted oil. Top 5 in 2024-25 — USA, China, UAE, Russia, Saudi Arabia.

questions.stem: India's foreign exchange reserves are managed by:

options.option_text: Ministry of Finance
Reserve Bank of India (under FEMA, 1999)
SEBI
Department of Commerce

questions.explanation: RBI manages forex reserves under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999 (replaced FERA, 1973 — much stricter regime). Reserves include foreign currency assets (mainly USD, EUR, GBP, JPY), gold (kept partially in BoE London + RBI Mumbai), SDR (IMF), and Reserve Tranche Position with IMF. As of mid-2025 — India's forex reserves ~$650-680 B (4th largest globally after China, Japan, Switzerland). RBI uses reserves to manage rupee volatility, fund import surges, service external debt.

questions.stem: In international trade terminology, 'dumping' occurs when a country exports goods at a price:

options.option_text: Higher than the domestic price to earn maximum foreign exchange
Lower than their normal value or cost in the exporting country
Fixed by bilateral agreement between the two trading nations
Subsidised exclusively for development of emerging market economies

questions.explanation: Dumping means exporting at below normal value (domestic price or cost of production), undercutting local producers in the importing country. Option A is the opposite—dumping is precisely about under-pricing, not over-pricing. Anti-dumping duties (like India's on several Chinese goods) are levied specifically to offset this practice under WTO rules.

questions.stem: Which of the following transactions is recorded under the Capital/Financial Account, NOT the Current Account, in India's Balance of Payments?

options.option_text: Remittances received from Indian workers employed overseas
Earnings from software and IT services exported to the USA
Foreign Direct Investment inflows into Indian manufacturing firms
Interest payments made on India's outstanding external loans

questions.explanation: FDI inflows represent cross-border capital movement and are recorded under the Financial Account of BoP. The Current Account covers trade in goods, trade in services, income, and current transfers. Options A and D are Current Account items (transfers and income respectively), and Option B (software services) is a services export under the Current Account.

questions.stem: India's RoDTEP scheme, which replaced the WTO-incompatible MEIS, provides eligible exporters with:

options.option_text: Duty-free import authorisations for raw materials used in exports
Transferable duty credit scrips refunding embedded domestic taxes
Direct cash subsidies credited into the exporter's bank account
Customs duty waivers on all imported capital goods for five years

questions.explanation: RoDTEP (Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products) remits central, state, and local taxes embedded in exported goods via transferable electronic duty credit scrips. MEIS was WTO-incompatible because it gave direct subsidies (Option C); RoDTEP is WTO-compliant as it only remits taxes already paid. Option A describes Advance Authorisation, a separate scheme entirely.

questions.stem: A country's 'Terms of Trade' (ToT) index is said to have IMPROVED when:

options.option_text: Import prices rise faster than export prices in world markets
The physical volume of exports exceeds the volume of its imports
Export prices rise relative to import prices, raising purchasing power
The trade deficit narrows sharply due to a fall in exchange rate

questions.explanation: Terms of Trade = (Export Price Index / Import Price Index) × 100. ToT improves when this ratio rises—each unit of export buys more imports, enhancing real purchasing power. Option A describes a worsening ToT. Option B confuses volume with prices—ToT is strictly a price-ratio concept, not a quantity comparison. Option D relates to trade balance adjustment, not terms of trade.

questions.stem: Under India's Foreign Trade Policy 2023–28, the 'Districts as Export Hubs' (DEH) initiative primarily seeks to:

options.option_text: Declare selected districts as Special Economic Zones with tax holidays
Identify district-level export-potential products and build local supply chains
Provide automatic export licences to all MSMEs in notified districts
Exempt district-based exporters from customs duty on capital equipment

questions.explanation: DEH creates district-level institutional mechanisms to identify products/services with export potential and develop action plans—essentially grassroots export promotion through DGFT. It does not confer SEZ status (A), grant automatic licences (C), or provide duty exemptions (D). Students commonly conflate DEH with SEZ policy or MSME export incentive schemes, making A and C effective distractors.

questions.stem: In India's Balance of Payments accounting, which of the following transactions creates a CREDIT (positive) entry in the Current Account?

options.option_text: An Indian firm purchasing equity shares of a foreign company worth $5 mn
Indian government repaying principal on an outstanding IMF loan tranche
Foreign tourists spending at Indian hotels, generating inward forex revenue
An Indian company paying dividends to its non-resident shareholders abroad

questions.explanation: BoP credit entries arise when India receives payments from non-residents. Foreign tourist spending = export of tourism services = Current Account credit. Option A is a capital outflow (Financial Account debit). Option B is repayment of a liability (Financial Account debit). Option D is an income payment to non-residents (Current Account debit, not credit). The core rule: inflow of foreign exchange → credit; outflow → debit.

questions.stem: The 'J-curve effect' in international trade predicts that immediately after a country's currency depreciates:

options.option_text: Export volumes surge instantly as foreign buyers rush to capitalise on it
Trade balance first worsens then improves as export/import volumes adjust
Import volumes fall sharply, eliminating the trade deficit within months
Domestic inflation offsets the currency gain, leaving trade balance flat

questions.explanation: After depreciation, import prices in domestic currency rise immediately (worsening trade balance in value terms) while export and import volumes respond slowly due to existing contracts and price inelasticity—tracing a 'J' shape over time. Option A confuses the long-run volume response with the short-run: volumes lag, they do not surge instantly. Option D describes Marshall-Lerner condition failure, a related but distinct concept from the J-curve.
